title: Two arrested after police officers hurt in brawl outside Glasgow bare-knuckle fighting event
description: Image source, Gregory HoareImage caption, Officers quickly arrived after young men were seen fighting on the Clyde Arc bridgeUpdated 3 hours agoTwo me
body: Image source, Gregory HoareImage caption, Officers quickly arrived after young men were seen fighting on the Clyde Arc bridgeUpdated 3 hours agoTwo men have been arrested and three police officers injured during a street disturbance outside a bare-knuckle fighting championship in Glasgow. Footage circulating on social media shows a group of men trading punches in the street outside  the Ovo Hydro where the event was held on Saturday evening.More than 20 police vehicles and a police helicopter converged on the area. Three officers were hurt, two of them requiring medical treatment, as they responded to the disorder. Police Scotland said two men, aged 32 and 27, had been arrested and charged with offences including assault, obstructing police and threatening and abusive behaviour. Figure caption, More than 20 police vehicles converged on the area outside Glasgow's Ovo Hydro after violence broke out in nearby streetsThousands of spectators had earlier gathered for the Bare Knuckle Fighting Championship (BKFC) event where Sean Weir from Wishaw defeated Leigh Cohoon from Manchester when the referee stopped the fight in the first round. At about 23:10, police said they received reports of a large disturbance in the Congress Road area outside the venue. Image caption, Police Scotland said three officers were injured, two of them requiring medical treatementCh Insp Paul Daley said: "Several officers were assaulted whilst carrying out their duties during disorder following an event at the Hydro in Glasgow on Saturday night."Violence against officers is disgraceful and will not be tolerated. Being assaulted is not part of the job and it's extremely fortunate they were not seriously injured."The two men who have been charged are expected to appear at Glasgow Sheriff Court on Monday. A third man was arrested and issued with a recorded police warning. Police said inquiries were continuing and that anyone found responsible "will be brought to justice". They have asked anyone with information about the disturbance to contact them., external

schema.headline: Two arrested after police officers hurt in brawl outside Glasgow bare-knuckle fighting event

title: Nandy rejects claims of politicising Remembrance Sunday after Erasmus row
description: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has rejected accusations of politicising Remembrance Sunday after being criticised for linking the event to the UK rejoin
body: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has rejected accusations of politicising Remembrance Sunday after being criticised for linking the event to the UK rejoining the European Union's Erasmus scheme.Her department announced on Saturday night that "as we mark Remembrance Sunday, Erasmus+ will give a new generation the chance to build connections across Europe".That sparked a backlash from the Conservatives, who said "veterans did not fight for a student exchange scheme" and accused her of making an "EU membership pitch".Nandy said she was "horrified" by the Tory response and insisted that the expanded EU scheme for study and work would help young Britons recognise wartime sacrifice.The UK is rejoining the scheme in January, six years after leaving it as part of the Brexit deal.On Saturday, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport drew comparisons between that scheme and events on Sunday to commemorate veterans who had died in conflict.Referring to the scheme, Nandy said in her department's press release: "As we remember the immense courage of those who served our country, we honour them by building the best opportunities for the next generation through closeness and collaboration with our allies."Conservative Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake described her comments as "tone deaf and frankly shameful" and called on Nandy to apologise.He said the bonds that veterans forged "run far deeper" than Erasmus."It is not a day for a Labour minister to try to make an EU membership pitch," he added.Reform leader Nigel Farage told the BBC: "For Lisa Nandy to use Remembrance Sunday to announce this and say it's all about peace, it's all about the war - I find that very, very poor taste."Peter Sharples, chief executive of the Veterans Institute, told the Telegraph that people should "just honour the fallen" on Remembrance Sunday rather than discussing "party political matters".Asked about the criticism on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Nandy stood by her initial remarks."It was Winston Churchill after the Second World War who talked about extending the hand of friendship across Europe and making sure that we honoured the legacy of that generation," she said.She said that after Brexit "we closed off opportunities for young people from this country to understand not just the impact that generation made here in the UK, but the way in which they went off and fought for the freedom of people across Europe".Asked to respond to accusations she had chosen Remembrance Sunday to "promote part of the new deal the government has done with the EU", Nandy said she was "not choosing today or any day actually to promote a deal with the EU".Pressed about linking the day to what the government believes are the cultural benefits of the scheme, Nandy said: "There was a time where that wouldn't have even raised an eyebrow as somehow political, it was just common sense - and it is common sense."The UK is paying £570m to join the expanded Erasmus+ scheme, external, which the government said was a 30% discount. It will include free year-abroad placements for UK university students and their European peers as well as cultural exchanges.The government said free train passes would be available for 18-year-olds to visit EU countries by themselves or with up to five friends.Youth groups will also get to do short exchanges in other countries, with a focus on areas of the country less engaged by Erasmus previously such as the north of England and Midlands, the government said.Applications will open for Erasmus+ later this month.Farage described Erasmus as a "terrible scheme" and "wildly expensive" compared to the Turing Scheme, which ministers introduced in 2021 as a post-Brexit alternative.He also criticised ongoing negotiations between the UK and the EU for a new youth mobility scheme ahead of a major summit on 20 November.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.But the EU's former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes.Nandy said on Sunday that most of the benefits of Brexit promised in 2016 "have not been realised" and "there are trade-offs and choices to be made" on Britain's future relationship with the EU.

schema.headline: Nandy rejects claims of politicising Remembrance Sunday after Erasmus row

title: 'Time is up': Nandy warns media industry to take abuse seriously in wake of Brand case
description: Abuse in the media industry is probably still happening as organisations are not doing enough to protect women, the culture secretary has warned in th
body: Abuse in the media industry is probably still happening as organisations are not doing enough to protect women, the culture secretary has warned in the wake of Russell Brand's conviction.Lisa Nandy told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "Time is up, it really is time for the media industry to take this seriously."She added that since entering government, "many people" from within the industry had reached out to her "to allege that things have happened to them".Brand was found guilty of rape and sexual assault after a four-week trial, following allegations from multiple women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.Nandy was asked whether she believed there was still exploitation and abuse within the media industry, following the Brand trial and cancellation of Channel 4 reality show Married at First Sight after the BBC revealed rape allegations. She said: "I do not see that much has changed in terms of the way that institutions in the media industry and across public life, including politics, deal with women who very bravely come forward to allege abuse."Nandy added that there was often no protection and a "very heavy cost" for women who speak up in industries such as media and politics, pointing to power imbalances and short-term contracts some staff members are given."Hand on heart, I can't say to you as the culture secretary that this is not happening today. In fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is," she said. Nandy said many had come forward from within the industry, including from the BBC.But she added that the BBC had been an "exemplar" in signing up to the industry body to protect whistleblowers - the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority - and urged other organisations to follow suit.A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster "has made a significant commitment to improve its culture, processes and standards"."Last year, following an independent culture review, we set out the behavioural expectations for everyone who works with or for the BBC and we were clear action would be taken if these were not met," the spokesperson added.

schema.headline: 'Time is up': Nandy warns media industry to take abuse seriously in wake of Brand case

title: Vinted and eBay could be included in under-16 social media ban, minister says
description: Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said.Lisa Nandy said
body: Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said.Lisa Nandy said the government was "looking seriously" at including the retailing websites in the social media ban "to keep children safe". The UK's social media ban for under-16s is set to come into force in March next year, with children barred from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.In response, eBay said it was looking forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". Vinted said it welcomed "open dialogue" with ministers and the regulator on the issue.Asked on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether the government was looking to ban under-16s from Vinted and eBay, Nandy said: "We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe."It came after the Sunday Times reported, external that the UK's social media ban was being expanded to include the popular second-hand online marketplaces.The move was due to fears that messaging functions on the platforms allowed strangers to groom children, according to the newspaper. It suggested similar reselling platforms, Depop and Facebook Marketplace, would also be included in the list of banned sites.Businesses and individuals sell a host of goods on eBay, which has been a major global player in the online reselling market for years. The platform states on its website that it currently requires all of its members to be over 18 years old because listings involve "entering into a contract".Vinted is aimed at over 18s, but its terms and conditions do allow parents or guardians to create accounts for their children, which must be used under parental supervision.The site, on which users mostly buy and sell unwanted clothes and other fashion items, has grown rapidly recently to reach 17 million UK users.A Vinted spokesperson said direct messaging was "part of how the platform works" but that it had a "zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content" and had moderation teams and tools to spot and remove "activity that breaks our rules"."When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities," they said.An eBay spokesperson said the company was "focused on providing a trusted and safe marketplace experience for our millions of customers"."While the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government," they added.The government announced it would ban under-16s accessing social media in June this year, with children prevented from accessing 10 of the biggest platforms.YouTube will also be banned for under-16s, but YouTube Kids - a version of the video-sharing app designed to be safe for children - will not be included in the measures.A complete list of affected platforms has not yet been released, but the government said it would cover those "whose purpose is to enable social interaction and which allow users to post material".That means platforms that have livestreaming or features that enable the potential for strangers to contact children will also be restricted, which includes gaming sites.It does not mean that Roblox, the biggest gaming site in the UK for those aged eight to 12, for example, will be banned for under-16s. However, certain features such as its chat function will be restricted.But Matthew Sinclair, a senior director at the Computer and Communications Industry Association, which represents tech companies, argued that ministers should prevent the rules having "scope creep".He said a restriction on messaging for under-16s "would not stop at social media and would reach into the services families depend on to stay in touch", and urged the government to "ensure any new restrictions are proportionate and effective."The UK's ban comes after a similar one was introduced in Australia last year.Many children there have found ways to get round it, but the UK has said it intends to take a tougher approach.In recent weeks, attention has turned to how a social media ban would be enforced. Last month, the communications regulator Ofcom set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.Rani Govender, head of online child safety at the NSPCC, said the "real question" going forward was how the government ensured age checks were effective."But effective age checks are only part of the solution," she added. "Tech companies must also be required to build child safety into every platform, device and AI tool, so children are protected from harmful and illegal content and only able to access age-appropriate services."

schema.headline: Vinted and eBay could be included in under-16 social media ban, minister says

title: Swansea mum tries to raise £2.95m for son's dementia treatment
description: The mum of a five-year-old boy with a rare form of dementia has to pay almost £3m for his life saving treatment.Tate McDaid, from Swansea, was diagnos
body: The mum of a five-year-old boy with a rare form of dementia has to pay almost £3m for his life saving treatment.Tate McDaid, from Swansea, was diagnosed with Sanfilippo Syndrome - a form of dementia that just over 100 UK children have - when he was four. In September, the first gene therapy to treat the condition in children was approved in the US.His mum Tammy said she spent "months praying" for its approval but discovered the treatment is to set cost £2.95 million per child, with it unclear how families outside the US can fund this.Health officials from Wales are currently talking to those in the US to see what potential access pathways there are for Tate."I was excited when the treatment initially got approved but then reality hit hard the next day," Tammy said.This was when she read the US price for the one-time treatment, external had been set at $3.95 million.Tammy contacted Ultragenyx, who developed the treatment, in the hope of understanding how families outside the US, who do not have health insurance there, will cover the costs."We understand what they are charging for American citizens, but they've got health insurance," she added."What is it for us in the UK? "Not even just the UK, but everyone else in the world looking for this treatment."Explaining how the US approved drug, FAYUVI, would work for families outside the US, Ultragenyx said: "There is not a single estimate we can provide for the total cost of care for an international patient, as those costs would depend on the patient's individual medical needs and the treating institution."The Society for Mucopolysaccharide Diseases, external, a charity which helps children living with Sanfilippo Syndrome, said about 140 children in the UK have the condition.There is currently no cure for Sanfilippo Syndrome Type A, also called Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (MPS III), but the new drug could delay its onset, and allow Tate to remain active for longer.The condition, described as "childhood Alzheimer's" or "childhood dementia" due to its neurodegenerative nature, causes the gradual loss of abilities, such as walking and eating.It can progress more rapidly after the age of five, which is why Tammy said "it's really a battle of time" for her to raise enough money to get her son the treatment that is not available yet in the UK.She said: "If a millionaire turned around tomorrow and gave us the money, we'd go to the US straight away."With Tate turning six this month, Tammy doesn't believe time is on their side."Tate is already shown signs of cognitive decline," she added."The older he gets the less the treatment will work and the more ability he will lose in the process. "I feel like we are at a turning point and I'm petrified."

schema.headline: Swansea mum tries to raise £2.95m for son's dementia treatment

title: Diwali 2026: Indians celebrate festival with lights and fireworks
description: Millions across India are celebrating Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colour
body: Millions across India are celebrating Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.Air pollution in the Indian capital Delhi has reached such hazardous levels that it is the most polluted Diwali festival in a decade. New measures to improve air quality do not seem to have been successful.India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks. In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are at reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.

schema.headline: Diwali 2026: Indians celebrate festival with lights and fireworks

title: Labubu sales are slumping. Is the craze over?
description: For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the q
body: For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more.Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.

schema.headline: Labubu sales are slumping. Is the craze over?

title: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
description: Figure caption, Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last monthByBethany Bellin BavariaPerched on a ridge high up in the
body: Figure caption, Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last monthByBethany Bellin BavariaPerched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.Image source, Galerie Bilderwelt/Getty ImagesImage caption, Adolf Hitler used the mountain retreat to welcome guestsBefore it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.Image source, Universal Images Group via Getty ImagesImage caption, Before it was burned down, the Kehlsteinhaus or Eagle's Nest had long been a tourist destination in BavariaAround 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history."It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police say the old Nazi retreat was largely destroyed by last month's fireBut Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus."We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed."We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".Image source, ERIC SCHWAB/AFPImage caption, After Hitler's downfall, US soldiers captured the mountain-top retreat and are seen relaxing here on 4 May 1945Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question"."I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era. With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

schema.headline: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat

title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline HalpertRepublicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that po
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline HalpertRepublicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy."There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away. It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency."There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist. "But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."Image source, Getty ImagesShould Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decadesDemocrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination."Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nominationOther rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race."It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said."But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."Figure caption, 'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shiftFollow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?

title: The BBC News app keeps you informed with live and breaking news you can trust
description: Depending on the contract you have, data charges may apply for accessing the internet on your mobile device.If you are not sure about the potential ch
body: Depending on the contract you have, data charges may apply for accessing the internet on your mobile device.If you are not sure about the potential charges, please ask your mobile network provider. You may find some costs are included in your existing price plan or that you can opt for a data package that gives reduced charges for accessing the internet.The BBC does not charge you to access mobile content.

title: Iran executes three men for 'armed unrest' after January protests
description: Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media.Hassan Dioband, H
body: Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media.Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran, Iran's state news agency Tasnim, external reported.The executions are the latest in a series linked to the protests, including those of people accused of having ties to Israel and the United States.The number of executions in Iran has increased since US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic began in late February.The protest movement initially sparked in December last year by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 of January.Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, and blamed the violence on "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the US and Israel.However foreign-based NGOs gave higher figures and the BBC received multiple accounts from Iranians of security forces opening fire on unarmed protesters.Tasnim reported that the three men were executed after the Supreme Court upheld their convictions and found them guilty of "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups".The damage allegedly included an electricity substation in Karaj which caused power outages in some areas.Dioband was arrested on 11 January after investigations identified him as a suspect in attacks on public property and incitement to violence.Ten others accused of taking part in the unrest under his supervision were later arrested.Reuters news agency reports that they received prison terms of 5 to 10 years.The latest executions in Iran come after the UN human rights chief Volker Türk said he was alarmed by the rise in death penalties.In August, Türk said at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests.Iran is thought to be the world's second-most prolific executioner after China. Last year, it put to death at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International.The human rights group said that was the highest figure on record since 1981 and included 45 executions of suspected dissidents on national security-related charges.

title: Duo-euthanasia: When your parents choose to die
description: Bas had planned a scenic route to the hospice, taking in Friesland's meadows and canals."I still remember the whole trip," he says. His mum was in the
body: Bas had planned a scenic route to the hospice, taking in Friesland's meadows and canals."I still remember the whole trip," he says. His mum was in the back seat and his dad sat beside him. At first, they talked. Els seemed resolute about their decision to opt for euthanasia."My mum was convinced, certain about doing it," Bas says. "But my dad was a little bit emotional."Jan asked his son if they were doing the right thing. Bas was thrown - he thought it would be his mum who might have doubts."My mum had always really enjoyed life," he says. "I remember she told me, 'I'd love to be 80 or maybe even 90 years old.'"But his father had been talking about euthanasia for more than a decade because of all the years of pain.In the car, Bas reassured his dad. Once Jan calmed down, they drove without speaking, listened to music and watched the scenery go by.Bas found a parking space."My dad said goodbye to my car - he liked my car, and he said, 'Good job', and 'thank you'."And then we walked inside," Bas says. "Imagine doing that - being in their shoes, taking that trip and that walk. It's so unreal."For the next two hours, the couple's family and friends came and went. They reminisced, and listened to music. At one point, it crossed Bas' mind to call a halt to the proceedings."I had a feeling - 'OK, let's leave… Let's step into the car and drive away,'" he says. "But I didn't want to bring anything up that would make them feel uncertain - I had supported the whole [euthanasia] process."Better to keep everybody calm, and take the moment to say goodbye."Where to get help- The Samaritans, external- Befrienders Worldwide, external- NHS Help for suicidal thoughts, external- BBC Action LineJust before 10:30am, doctors arrived to inject Jan and Els with the lethal medication that would kill them. The couple lay on hospital beds side by side. And in those final moments, before they lost consciousness, Bas witnessed his parents' closeness."I've seen them maybe three or four times in all my life walking hand in hand," he says. "But now they were laying there, hand in hand. And that gave me a really good feeling - they're really doing this together."Bas describes that first half hour after his parents stopped breathing as "a factual thing" - they weren't alive anymore."Then you realise what the situation is - that's an unimaginable feeling."In the hospice, sorrow hit Bas. He began to experience a profound loneliness."Grieving is a very, very deep thing to go through," he says, "and I don't have brothers and sisters - I really felt alone."If we've been brought up by two parents, when the first dies, we can share our memories and sadness with the other as part of the process of bereavement. But Jan and Els were both gone."It was like my legs were cut off," remembers Bas.His grief was physical too - he felt sick for four or five weeks. His body hurt."I would not really recommend this to others, and that's maybe a hard conclusion," he says. "It was maybe for them [my parents] the best option, but having lost them both at the same moment was very, very impactful."Among people planning to apply for euthanasia in the Netherlands, especially those with dementia like Els, choosing the right moment to end your life may be complicated.9,958 people in the Netherlands chose death by euthanasia in 2024427 of those who chose death by euthanasia in 2024 had dementia - six had advanced dementia108 people chose death by duo-euthanasia (54 pairs) that yearSource: Regional Euthanasia Review Committees (RTE)As well as demonstrating they are suffering unbearably, they must be assessed by doctors as still having the capacity to decide for themselves they want to die. This can cause immense distress in dementia patients thinking about euthanasia, explains Dr Rozemarijn van Bruchem, a geriatrician and ethicist at the Erasmus Medical Centre in Rotterdam."They think… I have that power right now, but now is too soon. But maybe next month is too late. So how do I decide at what point I need to start this process to see if I meet the criteria, to see if I can get euthanasia? And if I wait too long, might I have missed the window?"Dr van Bruchem says it's because euthanasia is legal in the Netherlands that her patients experience this anxiety. And they know permission for an assisted death in cases of advanced dementia is rare. In countries where euthanasia is prohibited, like the UK, people with dementia may face many challenges, but they rarely have to weigh these life-or-death options - as Els did.In 2024, she told the BBC that she and her husband couldn't wait because there was a chance her Alzheimer's would progress. And Jan was committed to dying with Els. He told the BBC that perhaps he was going too soon, but he had lived his life – his life was completed.Jan and Els were very aware of the burden their end-of-life decisions placed on their son. Bas attended all the meetings his parents had with their separate doctors during the euthanasia process. There were open family discussions. Often, we have regrets when a loved-one dies – especially about what may have been left unspoken. This didn't happen to Bas. Two days before Jan and Els' appointment at the hospice on Monday 3 June he wrote them a letter."It was about eight pages," Bas says. "I went to the campervan late in the evening on Saturday night. I read the whole letter to them. It was about our lives, thanking them for what they'd done."Jan and Els were deeply moved. And just as they rarely displayed affection to each other in public, they hadn't usually been demonstrative with their son either."You feel that they love you, but it's shown by doing stuff, not really saying it, or giving you a hug," says Bas. "My mum did [hug] more when she got dementia, but my dad never did – I never got a hug."That changed in the campervan on that last Saturday night. Jan hugged Bas."He did it after that letter.  It was maybe one of the best moments."Everything was said."

title: Ambika Mod: Ceiling is getting higher for South Asian actors
description: She has previously spoken about not having access to the same "privilege", external some of her fellow actors do when it comes to roles. Fans have que
body: She has previously spoken about not having access to the same "privilege", external some of her fellow actors do when it comes to roles. Fans have questioned why she hasn't gone on to appear in as many roles as her One Day co-star Leo Woodall, who's since appeared in major films including Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy and A24's Anthony Bourdain biopic, Tony.Addressing this remark, Mod tells Newsbeat she thinks "there's definitely an issue in this industry with systemic racism"."I think it is really hard for South Asian actors to really push through. "I feel like the glass ceiling is always getting higher and higher and higher."A report from the Creative Diversity Network, external suggested that representation of minority ethnic groups on and off-screen dropped slightly last year, after a few years of improvement.And similar research from media watchdog Ofcom , externalfound people from certain backgrounds are less well-represented across the UK broadcasting industry.It said "people from minority ethnic groups (across the industry as a whole) only account for 11% of those in senior management roles".It also found under-representation in creative, production and on-screen roles.Mod says she doesn't know if on-screen representation is changing, but says she "won't engage" with a role if she thinks its tokenistic or stereotypical."I've been very, very lucky in my career so far from very early on to play really complex, meaty roles and to have changed the narrative in many ways," she says."And I'm not looking to regress."And when it comes to considering what to take on next, she says she tries to follow advice Dame Emma Thompson once gave her: "There's no such thing as a career, there's only what you do next.""I'm always just trying to focus on what the new challenging thing is going to be, or cool people that I want to work with," she says."And also what's going to be fun, as well."Her latest role as Laila, a lawless agent of the covert Black Doves, attracted her as it subverted a lot of espionage genre tropes.The character is introduced in season two to assist Keira Knightley's agent Helen on a mission as the stakes get even higher for those working with the secretive organisation. Mod says it was "such a good time" working alongside Knightley and getting to do some extreme stunt sequences together. "Honestly, the main reason I wanted to do it was because of all the stunts," she says."Really badass but it was so much fun. "It was just so fun to take down an absolutely staggering number of men in every single episode." The thriller also has a dark humour to it, which aligns well with Mod who often brings a dry wit to her characters.Her comedic career goes back to when she was about 18, and while studying at Durham University she was part of its sketch comedy group.Despite having not done stand-up for about five years, she says she would "love" to do more comedy in the future."I do sometimes think about going back to it," she reveals."I have a lot of stories to tell."

schema.headline: Ambika Mod: Ceiling is getting higher for South Asian actors

title: We face paying £9,000 tax even though our second home is in a war zone
description: Image caption, Kateryna and Mattias have had to postpone their plans to buy a new homeByMunenyasha SigaukeBBC Scotland NewsA Ukrainian woman who fled
body: Image caption, Kateryna and Mattias have had to postpone their plans to buy a new homeByMunenyasha SigaukeBBC Scotland NewsA Ukrainian woman who fled to Scotland after Russia invaded her homeland has been told she could face a £9,000 property tax charge because she still owns a flat in Kyiv. Kateryna Stepanovych, 38, discovered the potential charge when she tried to buy a house in North Ayrshire with her Scottish partner Mattias Lindgren. The couple were told the Additional Dwelling Supplement (ADS) charge would apply because she already owned a property overseas. Kateryna bought the small flat in 2018, before Russia's invasion. She fled the war zone in 2023, leaving the property behind. Image source, Kateryna StepanovychImage caption, Kateryna says the 10-storey building in Kyiv where she has an apartment was hit by shrapnel in an attack in 2023The conflict has seen shrapnel strike the front of her 10-storey apartment building, damaging its exterior and a neighbouring property. Her own flat remained undamaged. "The fact that the property is still there is a miracle," Mattias said. The couple, who currently live in Stromness in Orkney, only became aware of the £9,000 charge when they put down an offer on the property they were planning to buy and Mattias looked through the paperwork from their solicitor. Unable to afford the additional cost, they had to withdraw their offer. Mattias said: "Why should we be punished with this tax for a property that's in a war zone?" Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Kyiv has come under regular attack since Russia invaded in 2022Under Revenue Scotland's rules, the Additional Dwelling Supplement Charge can see house buyers facing an additional 8% charge if they already own another property, including overseas.It was introduced by the Scottish government primarily to target people who are buying second or buy-to-let homes and is paid in addition to Land and Buildings Transaction Tax. The couple got in touch with Orkney MSP Liam McArthur in the summer after being told by their solicitors there was nothing they could do about the charge.McArthur then contacted Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth, who responded with a letter which stated that there are "no provisions within the legislation that allow either the Scottish government or Revenue Scotland to disapply ADS on a discretionary or case-by-case basis." Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, The couple's case was raised in the Scottish Parliament by Liam McArthurLib Dem MSP McArthur raised the couple's case in the Scottish Parliament on Tuesday, when he asked First Minister John Swinney whether he "agrees with me that this is surely not the intended purpose of the tax?" Swinney said he would ask Revenue Scotland to investigate the case, adding that he could understand why the rules had created the situation the couple were facing. Kateryna and Mattias had hoped to relocate this year, but are now considering renting while postponing their plans to buy. "It's been quite hard because we've had to rethink how we're approaching buying a property," Mattias said. Kateryna, who works in a factory, has found dealing with the issue particularly challenging because English is not her first language. "For me, it's difficult," she said, adding there was little else she could do beyond providing documents from Ukraine.The couple said they are now "biding our time" while exploring their options.

schema.headline: We face paying £9,000 tax even though our second home is in a war zone

title: Brent School Street fines at one location exceed £1m
description: A London council has issued more than £1m worth of penalty charge notices (PCNs) to drivers under a School Street scheme in less than two years.Brent
body: A London council has issued more than £1m worth of penalty charge notices (PCNs) to drivers under a School Street scheme in less than two years.Brent Council issued PCNs totalling £1.15m after introducing the scheme outside Manor School in Kensal Rise in November 2024, saying it would improve road safety and the environment.Ward councillor Barbara Want raised concerns about the scheme and claimed that the signs were "too high and not properly visible".Brent Council said the signs in place complied with Department for Transport guidelines, but that it had decided to install extra lower-level signs and gateway features to give more clarity to drivers.In the 21 months the scheme has been in place, the north-west London council has collected £54,799 on average per month, with the scheme only in place during term time.School Streets are being trialled across the borough to enforce road closures during drop-off and pick-up times, policed by CCTV cameras and mobile enforcement teams. Those caught face a PCN of £160, reduced to £80 if paid within 14 days.Previously, it was reported that 70,000 PCNs were issued in 12 months, at a rate of 384 per school day.In July 2025, the two cameras enforcing the scheme outside Manor School raised more than £107,000 in a single month, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.Want said: "For months I have been highlighting the huge volume of PCNs issued to drivers on the Manor School Street. The fact that it has raked in more than £1m in two years should have told them something wasn't right."It is failing children's safety if drivers are still using the road. I fear the scheme is more about revenue generation than improving road safety or air quality."Promise Knight, the council's cabinet member for cleaner streets, transport and public realm, said School Streets existed in the borough "to make the journey to and from school safer for children and families"."The purpose of the scheme is to protect children by reducing congestion and improving air quality."We will continue to review the scheme and make practical improvements where they can help drivers comply."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
